title: Investigate the Great Fire of London
description: A case file with maps and time-stamped evidence: inspect witnesses in different orders, distinguish seen from inferred, corroborate and assemble a defensible account with limits.
audience: Curious secondary learners and adults, including people uninterested in history
level: Introductory historical inquiry, no prior Great Fire study assumed

skills.title: Separate observation from inference with explicit uncertainty
skills.criterion: Relevant evidence, correct source distinction and explicit limit; no one-answer collapse of defensible interpretations

skills.title: Evaluate provenance, purpose and limits of a historical source
skills.criterion: Relevant evidence, correct source distinction and explicit limit; no one-answer collapse of defensible interpretations

skills.title: Corroborate independent accounts using maps and chronology
skills.criterion: Relevant evidence, correct source distinction and explicit limit; no one-answer collapse of defensible interpretations

skills.title: Build a defensible multi-causal explanation and acknowledge alternatives

nodes.title: The alert arrives
nodes.prompt: You are the night clerk. Pepys records that a servant woke him to news of a fire. Which line describes what his diary directly establishes?

options.text: The servant brought Pepys an alert.
options.feedback: Yes. The diary records the alert; its wording does not let Pepys see the first spark.

options.text: A spark from the baker’s oven started the fire.
options.feedback: That is a possible explanation of ignition, not something this alert establishes.

options.text: Foreign agents started the fire.
options.feedback: The alert supplies no evidence for an accusation.

hints: Ask what Pepys could personally see at the moment he was woken.
nodes.workedExample: The diary supports that Pepys was alerted; it cannot by itself establish the initial cause.
nodes.mechanism: An account can contain both direct observation and relayed news.

nodes.title: Two dispatches, two vantage points
nodes.prompt: Open the early reports in any order. Pin at least two, then write what the clerk could responsibly tell Londoners by morning.

activity.question: What is supported about the early fire, and what remains an inference?

sources.title: A diary hears, then sees
sources.origin: Samuel Pepys, diary; extract via The National Archives
sources.account: A servant alerted Pepys to a city fire. He later watched flames and strong wind from the river and Bankside, and urged that houses be pulled down.
sources.limit: His first alarm was secondhand. He did not see the first spark or establish the ignition cause.

sources.title: The Crown’s early report
sources.origin: London Gazette, licensed official newspaper; extract via The National Archives
sources.account: The report located the outbreak near Thames Street and London Bridge and emphasized the King’s orders to stop it.
sources.limit: It reports an early location and official response, not a tested cause; its public purpose may shape emphasis.

sources.title: A correspondent wants certainty
sources.origin: Lord Maynard to Joseph Williamson, from Eton; letter via The National Archives
sources.account: Maynard described stories reaching him about possible plots, but said he did not know what to believe and wanted a trustworthy account.
sources.limit: He was away from London and was relaying rumours, not inspecting the origin.

rubric: Names at least two sources and distinguishes first-hand from relayed or official reporting.
States a supported early location or observation without inventing ignition.
Names one relevant limitation or unanswered question.

hints: The Gazette’s proximity to the fire in time does not make it an eyewitness to ignition.
Compare what Pepys saw later with what he was told first.
nodes.workedExample: A cautious dispatch might report the Gazette’s location and Pepys’s later view, then say neither observed the first spark.
nodes.mechanism: Keeping a question open is a historical move, not a failure.

nodes.title: The later letter
nodes.prompt: A 9 September letter from Eton repeats alarming stories but says the writer does not know what to believe. What can it most securely show?

options.text: How uncertainty and rumours travelled beyond London.
options.feedback: Yes. Its author reports his uncertainty from Eton; the rumour is not verified by the letter.

options.text: That a plot caused the ignition.
options.feedback: Repeating an allegation does not establish its truth.

options.text: Exactly when Pudding Lane caught fire.
options.feedback: The letter was later and written away from London.

hints: Attend to where the writer was and whether he saw the event.
nodes.workedExample: The letter is direct evidence of Maynard’s uncertainty, not direct evidence of ignition.
nodes.mechanism: Provenance changes what a source can support.

debrief.title: Your first dispatch is filed
debrief.body: A first report can locate an event without explaining its ignition. Your written source claim remains open for human review.

nodes.title: The headline is loud
nodes.prompt: A pamphlet accuses foreign people of using fireballs. Before deciding whether to trust it, what would you ask first?

options.text: Who made this, when, and what independent record supports the allegation?
options.feedback: Yes. Provenance and corroboration are the first checks for an extraordinary accusation.

options.text: Is the accusation exciting enough to remember?
options.feedback: Vividness is not evidence.

options.text: Can I find the same words copied in another pamphlet?
options.feedback: Copying one allegation would not be independent corroboration.

hints: Think about the writer’s purpose and independent evidence.
nodes.workedExample: Record the pamphlet as a contemporary allegation, then check its claims against independently produced records.
nodes.mechanism: A source’s existence proves a claim circulated; its content still needs evaluation.

nodes.title: Build a provenance file
nodes.prompt: The Gazette, Whitehall, a private diary, a distant letter and a sensational pamphlet all speak differently. Pin at least two and compare what they can support.

activity.question: Whose purpose and vantage point change the weight you give their account?

sources.title: The Crown’s early report
sources.origin: London Gazette, licensed official newspaper; extract via The National Archives
sources.account: The report located the outbreak near Thames Street and London Bridge and emphasized the King’s orders to stop it.
sources.limit: It reports an early location and official response, not a tested cause; its public purpose may shape emphasis.

sources.title: A diary hears, then sees
sources.origin: Samuel Pepys, diary; extract via The National Archives
sources.account: A servant alerted Pepys to a city fire. He later watched flames and strong wind from the river and Bankside, and urged that houses be pulled down.
sources.limit: His first alarm was secondhand. He did not see the first spark or establish the ignition cause.

sources.title: The official retrospective
sources.origin: Whitehall printed account; transcript via The National Archives
sources.account: The account connected rapid spread to close wooden buildings and an easterly wind, described attempts to demolish houses, and defended the government’s response.
sources.limit: It was issued by the government after the event and partly serves to justify officials; compare its claims with other witnesses.

sources.title: A correspondent wants certainty
sources.origin: Lord Maynard to Joseph Williamson, from Eton; letter via The National Archives
sources.account: Maynard described stories reaching him about possible plots, but said he did not know what to believe and wanted a trustworthy account.
sources.limit: He was away from London and was relaying rumours, not inspecting the origin.

sources.title: A dramatic printed accusation
sources.origin: Anonymous contemporary pamphlet; transcript via The National Archives
sources.account: Several letters alleged that French or Dutch people used fireballs. The pamphlet also gave conflicting timing and identity details.
sources.limit: The allegations are evidence of rumour and prejudice, not proof that any accused group caused the fire.

rubric: Identifies creator, date, position or audience for the chosen records.
Treats allegations about French or Dutch people as unverified claims, not established fact.
Compares at least two independent origins and states a limit of each.

hints: An official record can be useful while still selecting what it emphasizes.
A diary can offer a personal observation without proving every reported detail.
nodes.workedExample: One defensible comparison is that Pepys observed later spread, while Whitehall offered an official explanation after the fire; neither witnessed ignition.
nodes.mechanism: This is an open judgement. Your draft needs a human reader to assess it.

nodes.title: A fresh source label
nodes.prompt: You find an official report written six days after the fire. It describes wind and closely built wooden houses, then defends government action. Which label best fits?

options.text: Contemporary retrospective account with a possible institutional interest.
options.feedback: Yes. It is close in time, but its purpose and author matter.

options.text: Neutral eyewitness proof of the first spark.
options.feedback: The report was issued later and does not observe ignition.

options.text: A modern historian’s synthesis.
options.feedback: It was created in 1666, though it looks back at the event.

hints: Classify when it was made and why, separately.
nodes.workedExample: The Whitehall account is contemporary primary material about an official interpretation, not neutral direct sight of the start.
nodes.mechanism: Source type is about creation and context, not simple trust/distrust.

debrief.title: The source desk stays open
debrief.body: The files reveal different purposes and vantage points. A dramatic account is evidence of a claim being made, not necessarily of the event claimed.

nodes.title: A map with a trap
nodes.prompt: An archive map shows ruined streets, but was surveyed after the fire. What question can that map answer most directly?

options.text: Which streets and landmarks were recorded in the ruined area afterward.
options.feedback: Yes. It is a post-fire survey, so its strongest claim concerns recorded damage.

options.text: The exact hour each street caught fire.
options.feedback: A later static survey does not timestamp each flame front.

options.text: Whether a particular person lit the first flame.
options.feedback: Damage mapping cannot identify an individual cause.

hints: Read the survey date before reading damage as a timeline.
nodes.workedExample: A post-fire map is excellent evidence for surveyed ruins, not a clock for the spreading fire.
nodes.mechanism: Date the source, not just the event it depicts.

nodes.title: Walk the evidence map
nodes.prompt: The sketch puts the river, bridge, Pudding Lane, Bankside and St Paul’s in broad relation. The cards date accounts and a later survey. Pin independent clues and write a cautious route claim.

activity.question: What broad spread can the accounts support, and which route detail remains unproved?

sources.title: The Crown’s early report
sources.origin: London Gazette, licensed official newspaper; extract via The National Archives
sources.account: The report located the outbreak near Thames Street and London Bridge and emphasized the King’s orders to stop it.
sources.limit: It reports an early location and official response, not a tested cause; its public purpose may shape emphasis.

sources.title: A diary hears, then sees
sources.origin: Samuel Pepys, diary; extract via The National Archives
sources.account: A servant alerted Pepys to a city fire. He later watched flames and strong wind from the river and Bankside, and urged that houses be pulled down.
sources.limit: His first alarm was secondhand. He did not see the first spark or establish the ignition cause.

sources.title: A view from across the river
sources.origin: John Evelyn, diary; extract via The National Archives
sources.account: From Bankside, Evelyn saw a large sweep of burning near the waterside and described a fierce easterly wind.
sources.limit: His distant view supports broad extent, not a street-by-street path or the first ignition.

sources.title: Why the survey exists
sources.origin: Charles II’s instruction; record via The National Archives
sources.account: The King commissioned Hollar and Sandford to plan and survey the City as it stood after the fire, with the ruins described.
sources.limit: The commission explains purpose, but is neither a damage map itself nor evidence about how the blaze began.

sources.title: A survey after the flames
sources.origin: Wenceslaus Hollar / City surveyors; map via The National Archives
sources.account: The survey shows streets and ruined areas after the fire, including the Thames, London Bridge area and St Paul’s.
sources.limit: Blank ruin areas do not timestamp when each street burned or show flame direction during the event.

rubric: Uses dated observations and the post-fire survey without treating them as interchangeable snapshots.
Corroborates a broad place or direction with more than one independent origin.
Notes that this schematic is not to scale and cannot establish precise times or speeds.

hints: The map is a place index; the dated accounts carry time clues.
Evelyn’s Bankside view and Hollar’s later survey answer different questions.
nodes.workedExample: Evelyn’s 3 September view and Pepys’s account support broad extent near the river; Hollar’s later survey shows ruins, but none pins each street to an exact hour.
nodes.mechanism: A useful map claim is deliberately bounded.

nodes.title: A new label on the survey
nodes.prompt: The King ordered a survey on 10 September to record the City after the fire. Which inference survives this date check?

options.text: The resulting map can show surveyed ruins; it cannot alone date each street’s burning.
options.feedback: Yes. Commission and survey dates limit temporal claims.

options.text: Every white block burned on 2 September.
options.feedback: The survey cannot date individual blocks this way.

options.text: The commission proves the first ignition happened at St Paul’s.
options.feedback: The commission concerns ruins and mapping, not ignition.

hints: What did the commission ask the surveyors to record?
nodes.workedExample: The 10 September commission establishes a post-fire purpose for the survey.
nodes.mechanism: Source creation date is part of map interpretation.

debrief.title: The route remains a hypothesis
debrief.body: Your map links places and source dates, but no surviving survey in this case file plays back the flames minute by minute.

nodes.title: The easy story is too neat
nodes.prompt: A colleague says, “One rumour explains everything.” What should a careful investigator do first?

options.text: Separate ignition from spread, and seek independent evidence for each claim.
options.feedback: Yes. Different questions need different sources and may have different levels of certainty.

options.text: Treat the loudest contemporary pamphlet as the answer.
options.feedback: A contemporary allegation still needs corroboration.

options.text: Assume a later damage map identifies the culprit.
options.feedback: A ruin survey does not establish who or what ignited the fire.

hints: Try splitting “why” into ignition, rapid spread and response.
nodes.workedExample: A defensible explanation can be strong on spread and cautious on the first spark.
nodes.mechanism: Good history distinguishes what is known from what remains uncertain.

nodes.title: Convene the case conference
nodes.prompt: Choose any two or more source files. Draft a multi-causal account of spread and assess the accusations about ignition; cite the limits of your evidence.

activity.question: What account would you defend to a sceptical colleague, and what would you still investigate?

sources.account: Several letters alleged that French or Dutch people used fireballs. The pamphlet also gave conflicting timing and identity details.

sources.title: A modern synthesis
sources.origin: London Museum, modern public history article
sources.account: The museum describes dry conditions, east winds, close buildings and combustible goods as factors in spread; it treats the precise ignition as uncertain.
sources.limit: A synthesis combines earlier evidence; it is not a direct observation made in 1666.

rubric: Makes a claim about spread supported by at least two independent records, for example wind plus closely built combustible streets.
Separates the uncertain first ignition from better-attested conditions of spread and attempts to stop it.
Handles the pamphlet’s accusations as allegations and does not blame a group without corroboration.
Names a source limit, missing perspective or follow-up question.

hints: Look for agreement across an eyewitness and a differently produced record.
Rumour of a plot is evidence of fear and prejudice unless independently supported.
nodes.workedExample: A careful account can connect wind and close buildings to rapid spread while leaving the exact ignition unsettled and refusing to promote an unsupported accusation.
nodes.mechanism: Your claim will need a human reader; the app only records your reflection.

nodes.title: Challenge from the editor
nodes.prompt: The editor asks whether the post-fire survey and the pamphlet together prove who started the fire. Which reply is defensible?

options.text: No. The survey records ruins and the pamphlet records an allegation; neither proves a culprit.
options.feedback: Yes. Each can be useful without answering the ignition question.

options.text: Yes. A map plus a printed accusation is independent proof.
options.feedback: The records answer different questions; the map does not corroborate the culprit claim.

options.text: Yes, because both were made close to 1666.
options.feedback: Proximity in time alone does not establish the alleged act.

hints: Ask what each source was actually made to record.
nodes.workedExample: Two sources are not corroboration when one does not address the claim.
nodes.mechanism: The bounded method check is separate from the open historical claim.

debrief.title: The case is yours to defend
debrief.body: Your claim, source pins and rubric reflection are stored in your local case file. A teacher or course owner still needs to judge the quality of your historical argument.
